title: Long‐Term Climate Simulations Using the IITM Earth System Model (IITM‐ESMv2) With Focus on the South Asian Monsoon

venue.name: Journal of Advances in Modeling Earth Systems

abstract: Abstract Long‐term climate simulations are performed using the IITM Earth System Model version 2 (IITM‐ESMv2), a sequel to the earlier version (IITM‐ESMv1), to assess climate variability and change with a special focus on the South Asian monsoon. Substantial improvements are incorporated in IITM‐ESMv2 to obtain a radiatively balanced global climate modeling framework. The IITM‐ESMv2 includes time‐varying aerosol forcing and land‐use land‐cover changes. Multicentury simulations corresponding to preindustrial and present‐day conditions show major improvements in capturing key aspects of time‐mean atmosphere and ocean large‐scale circulation. Representations of the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation and poleward ocean heat transport, and major global climate drivers are superior to ESMv1. Teleconnections of the South Asian monsoon with climate drivers such as the El‐Niño–Southern Oscillation (ENSO) and the Indian Ocean Dipole (IOD) are found to be more robust in IITM‐ESMv2, thus leading to improved simulation of South Asian monsoon and its variability. The IITM‐ESMv2 takes a novel pursuit from India to contribute in the Intergovernmental Panel for Climate Change (IPCC) sixth assessment report (AR6).
problem: The previous climate model version, IITM-ESMv1, suffered from a significant radiative imbalance and phenomenological shortcomings, such as a weak Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation, which limited its reliability for accurately simulating long-term climate variability, especially for the South Asian monsoon.
method: The paper presents an improved Earth System Model (IITM-ESMv2) that corrects radiative imbalance and enhances climate simulations by incorporating updated aerosol forcing, a revised deep convection scheme, a dynamic sea-ice model, and improved flux exchange parameterizations between components.
task: The task is to assess the capabilities of the IITM Earth System Model version 2 (IITM-ESMv2) for simulating long-term climate variability and change, with a special focus on the South Asian monsoon, and to document its improvements over the previous version.

innovation: This paper presents the IITM-ESMv2, the first Indian climate model contributing to the IPCC AR6, which demonstrates substantial improvements in simulating the South Asian monsoon and key global climate drivers, such as AMOC, compared to its predecessor.

Substantial improvements are incorporated in IITM-ESMv2 to obtain a radiatively balanced global climate modeling framework.
The IITM-ESMv2 takes a novel pursuit from India to contribute in the Intergovernmental Panel for Climate Change (IPCC) sixth assessment report (AR6).

Teleconnections of the South Asian monsoon with climate drivers such as the El-Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) and the Indian Ocean Dipole (IOD) are found to be more robust in IITM-ESMv2, thus leading to improved simulation of South Asian monsoon and its variability.

Teleconnections of the South Asian monsoon with climate drivers such as the El-Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) and the Indian Ocean Dipole (IOD) are found to be more robust in IITM-ESMv2, thus leading to improved simulation of South Asian monsoon and its variability.

An earlier version of IITM-ESM (referred as the IITM-ESMv1) was developed by transforming a state-of-the-art seasonal prediction model, Climate Forecast System version 2 (CFSv2, Saha et al., 2010), into a model suitable for simulating long-term climate (Swapna et al., 2015).

kg_extraction_triplets.paragraph: While the IITM-ESMv1 successfully captured the dominant modes of climate variability such as the El Nino Southern Oscillation (ENSO) and Pacific decadal oscillation (PDO) which have marked teleconnections with the large-scale circulation and South Asian monsoon rainfall (Krishnan & Sugi, 2003; Shukla & Paolino, 1983), there were setbacks i.e., a century long IITM-ESMv1 simulations showed a significant radiative imbalance of about 6 W m¯² and there are phenomenological shortcomings, such as weakening of the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC).

The atmosphere component of ESMv2 is a spectral general circulation model, Global Forecast System (GFS, Moorthi et al., 2001) based on the National Centre for Environmental Prediction (NCEP, Saha et al., 2014b).

The GFS model used in ESMv2 has a spectral triangular truncation of 62 waves (T62) in the horizontal (~2° grid) and finite differencing in the vertical with 64 sigma-pressure hybrid layers with top model layer extending up to 0.2 hPa.

The GFS version used in ESMv2 is similar to ESMv1 as discussed in (Swapna et al., 2015), with the following changes: 1. The revised Simplified Arakawa-Schubert (SAS) scheme (Han & Pan, 2011) is implemented for parameterizing deep cumulus convection.

The sea ice component of ESMv2 is the Sea Ice Simulator (SIS, Winton, 2000). SIS is a dynamical model with three vertical layers, one snow and two ice, and five ice thickness categories. More description about SIS can be obtained from (Delworth et al., 2006).

The GFS version used in ESMv2 is similar to ESMv1 as discussed in (Swapna et al., 2015), with the following changes: ... 3. Fractional grid implementation for the exchange of fluxes between atmosphere and other component models.

kg_extraction_triplets.target_entity_instance: heating by turbulent kinetic energy (TKE) dissipation
kg_extraction_triplets.paragraph: The GFS version used in ESMv2 is similar to ESMv1 as discussed in (Swapna et al., 2015), with the following changes: ... 4. The heating by turbulent kinetic energy (TKE) dissipation is included in the model.
The ocean model used in ESMv2 is the GFDL Modular Ocean Model Version 4p1 (MOM4p1, Griffies et al., 2009).
The MOM4p1 is a hydrostatic model configured here using the Boussinesq approximation and a rescaled geopotential vertical coordinate.
The zonal resolution is 1º and the meridional resolution is 0.33° between 10°S and 10°N and gradually becoming 1º poleward of 30°S and 30°N with 50 vertical levels.

Key physical parameterizations include a KPP surface boundary layer scheme similar to that of (Large et al., 1994), which computes vertical diffusivity, vertical viscosity, and nonlocal transport as a function of the flow and surface forcing.
The interactive ocean biogeochemistry module in MOM4p1 is also included in ESMv2.

The preindustrial (1850) and present-day (2005) control integrations are conducted, differing in the atmospheric trace gas, aerosol concentrations, insolation, and distribution of land cover types according to 1850 and 2005 conditions.

kg_extraction_triplets.target_entity_instance: TOA radiation balance of 0.85 W m¯²
kg_extraction_triplets.paragraph: The net radiative imbalance (downward shortwave- upward shortwave - outgoing longwave) at the top-of-the-atmosphere (TOA) showed a mean value of 0.85 W m¯²; while 6 Wm-2 imbalance was seen in ESMv1 (Swapna et al., 2015). The energy imbalance at the surface is 0.86 W m¯², thus the imbalance in the atmosphere is about 0.01 Wm-2. The TOA radiation balance in ESMv2 is in good agreement with the estimates from other state-of art climate models (Forster et al., 2013).

The overall pattern of bias is similar in both the models, which exhibit a warm SST bias in the Southern Ocean. Increase in shallow convective clouds is known to enable large reductions in shortwave radiation biases, resulting in cooling of Southern Ocean (see Kay et al. 2016). It is noticed that the Southern Ocean warm bias is more in ESMv2 as compared to ESMv1.
Similarly, the cold SST bias in the tropical regions in ESMv2 may be related to biases in simulation of low-level clouds (supporting information Figure S5c).
The ESMv2 show dry bias over the equatorial Pacific, Amazon region and Southeast Asia, while dry bias over Indian region and excess rainfall bias over the western Pacific is reduced in ESMv2.

A pattern correlation of mean summer monsoon rainfall (June-September) between the historical simulation of CMIP5 models and observation is performed over south and southeast Asian (65°E-140°E, 10°S-45°N) domain and the Indian region, and the statistics is shown on a Taylor diagram (Figure 10a). It can be seen that CMIP5 models are performing better over the bigger domain of south and southeast Asia in capturing the spatial pattern of mean seasonal rainfall with a reasonably good correlation (>0.5) against GPCP data. The ESMv2 also shows greater fidelity in capturing mean monsoon characteristics over this region with a correlation of 0.72 and standard deviation 1.03.

It can be seen that CMIP5 models are performing better over the bigger domain of south and southeast Asia in capturing the spatial pattern of mean seasonal rainfall with a reasonably good correlation (>0.5) against GPCP data. However, over the Indian land region, only 12 models show relatively better skill with correlations greater than 0.5 and standard deviation between 0.8 and 1.2 against GPCP data. It is noteworthy to see that ESMv2 shows relatively better skill with a correlation of 0.6 and standard deviation 0.9.

On interannual and longer time-scales, the variability of the Indian and Asian monsoon is strongly linked with the ENSO. The Indian monsoon rainfall tends to be below normal in the developing phase of ENSO. Many of the past studies have delineated the role of ENSO on Indian Summer Monsoon rainfall (ISMR) variability (Saith & Slingo, 2006; Sikka & Gadgil, 1980; Rajeevan & Pai, 2007; Rasmusson et al., 1982; Walker & Bliss, 1932). Observational estimates of rainfall shows that India tends to experience a below-normal monsoon during an El Niño or warm Pacific event and above-normal monsoon during a La Niña or cold Pacific event (Angell, 1981; Ropelewski & Halpert 1987; Sikka, 1980; Walker, 1924).
The variance explained by the EOF1 from ESMv2 is slightly higher (56%) than ESMv1 (52%), compared to the variance explained by HadISST (62%).

To understand the teleconnection of IOD with the India summer monsoon rainfall, the simultaneous correlation of SST anomalies in the eastern box of IOD (90°E–110°E, 0°–10°S) with summer monsoon rainfall is computed and is shown in Figure 13. It is known that the convection over eastern equatorial Indian Ocean suppress the rainfall over India through altering the regional Hadley cell (Krishnan et al., 2006, Sreejith et al., 2015) and the IOD related cold SST anomalies in eastern equatorial Indian Ocean enhance the monsoon trough (Annamalai, 2010) and induces anomalous moisture transport from the southeastern equatorial Indian Ocean and enhance the monsoon precipitation over the Bay of Bengal and the Indo-Gangetic plains (Behera et al., 1999).

The first version of the model, IITM Earth System Model v1 (IITM ESMv1), developed by transforming the Climate Forecast System (CFSv2, Saha et al., 2010) from the National Center for Environmental Prediction (NCEP) into a long-term climate model, captured the distribution of observed sea surface temperature and dominant modes of climate variability and teleconnections associated with the South Asian monsoon.
To improve the representation of deep convection over the tropical regions, the revised Arakawa Schubert convection scheme (Han & Pan, 2011) is incorporated in the atmospheric model.
